paragraphs: Sparse Bayesian learning seeks explanations that use relatively few nonzero coefficients in a probabilistic linear model. It encourages this sparsity through a prior on the coefficients. The paper addresses a theoretical weakness of classical algorithms: their optimization procedures lack essential guarantees that the iterations converge.

The proposed method reorganizes the marginal likelihood objective using auxiliary functions and the concave-convex procedure. This produces an iterative Min-Min optimization scheme in which hyperparameters governing both the sparsity prior and the noise level can be updated analytically. The approach therefore treats uncertainty about noise as part of the optimization alongside the parameters controlling sparse representations.

The authors prove global convergence of the procedure to a local minimum or a saddle point. Here, global convergence does not mean finding the globally best solution. Their simulation and real-world examples also show better sparse representation results than classical SBL algorithms, across signal recovery, system identification, and kernel regression. The contribution combines a more firmly justified optimization procedure with demonstrated practical improvements.
icml-2024-an-iterative-min-min-optimizat.tldr: An iterative sparse Bayesian learning algorithm analytically updates prior and noise hyperparameters with guaranteed convergence to a local minimum or saddle point.

paragraphs: Estimating where someone is looking from an entire face presents difficulties for existing self-supervised gaze methods developed around eye images. The paper identifies problems in both major approaches: contrastive methods struggle with data augmentation in this setting, while generative methods can reach trivial solutions because their internal semantic representations lack explicit constraints.

BeCa combines an autoencoder with a contrastive learning component. The autoencoder supplies the generative approach, while the contrastive component explicitly regularizes the representation of gaze. The authors also introduce InfoMSE, a replacement for the usual mean squared reconstruction error. Its purpose is to reduce the mismatch between reconstructing an image and learning a representation useful for gaze estimation.

Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art unsupervised gaze methods across extensive datasets, including images from uncontrolled scenes. The improvements appear both when training and testing within a dataset and when evaluating across datasets. These findings support combining reconstruction with representation constraints to address full-face gaze estimation, rather than relying on either learning approach alone.
icml-2024-bootstrap-autoencoders-with-co.tldr: BeCa combines autoencoding, contrastive regularization, and a revised reconstruction loss to improve self-supervised full-face gaze estimation.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate strong images, but their performance depends heavily on access to substantial training data. Transferring a pretrained generator offers a way to work with fewer examples. However, techniques developed for generative adversarial networks do not readily carry over to diffusion models, whose generation process involves repeated denoising across many timesteps.

The paper introduces ANT, a transfer learning method designed around those diffusion-specific requirements. It combines similarity-guided training, which uses a classifier to assist transfer, with adversarial noise selection. The latter adaptively chooses targeted noise according to the input image. Together, these strategies change both how transfer is guided and how noise is selected during learning.

In few-shot image generation experiments, the authors report that ANT is efficient and produces better image quality and diversity than the GAN-based and diffusion-based methods included in their comparisons. The findings support adapting transfer learning to the mechanics of diffusion itself. They show that both guidance from image similarity and image-dependent noise selection can form part of an effective approach when target data is scarce.
icml-2024-bridging-data-gaps-in-diffusio.tldr: ANT improves few-shot diffusion image generation through classifier-guided transfer and noise selection tailored to each input image.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained vision-language model usually requires access to its parameters. That access may be unavailable when a model owner exposes only prompts and predictions. CraFT addresses adaptation in this black-box setting, learning how to interact with the model and improve its outputs using only the permitted input and output interface.

CraFT has two trainable modules. One learns text prompts, and the other refines the resulting predictions through residual adjustments. An additional prediction-consistency loss helps align their optimization, while a collaborative training algorithm coordinates their learning. This makes adaptation a joint problem of choosing useful prompts and correcting the predictions those prompts produce.

Experiments cover few-shot classification on 15 datasets. The authors report a gain of about 12% with 16-shot datasets using 8,000 queries. They also report faster training and a deployment memory footprint of roughly one eightieth of the white-box comparison, with a reported performance sacrifice of 1.62%. These results show a practical adaptation tradeoff when direct access to a model's weights is unavailable.
icml-2024-connecting-the-dots-collaborat.tldr: CraFT adapts black-box vision-language models by jointly learning prompts and prediction refinements, with strong reported few-shot results and low deployment memory use.

paragraphs: Physical symmetries describe how a system's behavior relates across transformations. Departures from those symmetries can reveal meaningful changes in the system. This paper studies how neural networks can learn such departures from data, making asymmetry something to investigate rather than simply treating it as an obstacle to modeling.

The authors use relaxed group convolutions, which allow flexibility in how strongly a network respects a symmetry. They provide theoretical and empirical evidence that this approach can preserve the greatest degree of equivariance compatible with the observations. Equivariance means that a transformation of the input produces a corresponding transformation of the output. Relaxing it allows data to reveal where that relationship breaks.

The paper applies several architectures to crystal phase transitions, broken isotropy and homogeneity in turbulent flow, and broken time-reversal symmetry in pendulum systems. The discovered factors are reported to be interpretable and physically meaningful. The contribution is therefore both a modeling technique and a way to identify subtle departures from symmetry in the physical systems examined.
icml-2024-discovering-symmetry-breaking-.tldr: Relaxed group convolutions learn physically meaningful symmetry breaking while retaining the degree of equivariance supported by the data.

paragraphs: Event cameras offer low latency and high dynamic range, making them attractive for fast motion and difficult lighting. Reconstructing a three-dimensional scene from their output is challenging because the event stream is sparse and lacks absolute color information. EvGGS tackles reconstruction using only event inputs, representing the scene with three-dimensional Gaussians.

The framework connects depth estimation, intensity reconstruction, and Gaussian regression in a cascade. A joint loss trains these components collaboratively so their learning can support one another. Reconstruction happens through a feedforward process, and the framework can handle unseen cases without retraining. The authors also introduce a dataset containing objects with different materials and calibrated grayscale images, depths, camera poses, and silhouettes.

Experiments show that joint training significantly improves over training the components separately. The method also exceeds all compared baselines in reconstruction quality and depth and intensity prediction, while delivering rendering speed the authors describe as satisfactory. These findings support coordinated learning as a useful way to extract complementary scene information from event streams.
icml-2024-evggs-a-collaborative-learning.tldr: EvGGS jointly learns depth, intensity, and Gaussian scene representations to reconstruct unseen scenes directly from event-camera inputs without retraining.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks typically represent relationships by passing messages between connected nodes. This paper proposes a different starting point: convert the graph into a set of independent points, then learn from that set. The conversion is bijective, so the change in representation preserves the graph information rather than discarding its connections.

This allows set encoders to serve as graph learners and broadens the available architecture choices. For transformers, it also provides a principled way to supply graph structure without relying on heuristic positional or structural encodings. The authors build a Point Set Transformer, or PST, that takes the converted point set as its input.

The theoretical analysis establishes stronger expressivity than existing GNNs for the studied tasks of counting short-range substructures and representing long-range shortest-path distances. Experiments also support PST's real-world performance. A separate encoder based on Deepset achieves performance comparable to representative GNNs, showing that the conversion is useful beyond transformers. The central result is a structure-preserving bridge from graph learning to set learning.
icml-2024-graph-as-point-set-584baf06c8.tldr: A lossless graph-to-point-set conversion enables set encoders to learn graph representations, with strong theoretical and empirical results for a dedicated transformer.

paragraphs: Instance attribution explains a model prediction by assigning a score to each training example. A basic question is whether an example is judged helpful or harmful. This paper asks how stable that judgment remains when the dataset is resampled, introducing a robustness criterion focused on the sign of the attribution score.

The authors show theoretically and empirically that popular leave-one-out attribution methods lack this robustness. Shapley values behave substantially better, but computing them is more expensive. To make that alternative practical, the paper introduces FreeShap, an approximation based on the neural tangent kernel that avoids fine-tuning during attribution.

Empirical results show FreeShap outperforming other methods on instance attribution and on data removal, data selection, and incorrect-label detection. The authors also extend their approach to large language models. The significance is that useful attribution requires more than a score for one fixed dataset: its helpful-or-harmful interpretation should withstand changes in the sampled data. FreeShap addresses that concern while reducing the computational burden of Shapley-based explanations.
icml-2024-helpful-or-harmful-data-fine-t.tldr: FreeShap approximates Shapley attribution without fine-tuning, addressing the instability of helpful-or-harmful judgments under dataset resampling.

paragraphs: Value iteration networks incorporate a differentiable planning module into a neural network, allowing planning behavior to be learned end to end. Their difficulty with long-term planning comes partly from the challenge of training very deep versions of that module. This paper adapts highway value iteration to improve how information and learning signals travel through the network.

The resulting planning module adds three components. An aggregate gate creates skip connections across layers. An exploration module increases the diversity of information and gradient flow across spatial dimensions. A filter gate is designed to keep that exploration safe. Together, these additions address long-term credit assignment: learning how earlier planning computations contribute to later outcomes.

The authors report that highway VINs can be trained with hundreds of layers using standard backpropagation. On tasks requiring hundreds of planning steps, these deep networks outperform traditional VINs and several advanced, very deep neural networks. The findings connect better information flow during training with the ability to learn planning computations over substantially longer horizons in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2024-highway-value-iteration-networ.tldr: Highway value iteration networks use gates and exploration components to train hundreds of planning layers effectively for long-horizon tasks.

paragraphs: When data is missing not at random, the observed records may not uniquely determine the quantity researchers want to estimate. This is an identification problem, which arises before deciding how to calculate an estimate. Standard approaches generally need strong assumptions about the process producing the missing observations.

The paper instead supplements the original dataset with an auxiliary dataset whose missingness is at random. Its central result is that the combined information can identify a parameter even when neither dataset identifies it on its own. The authors establish this result under two complementary sets of assumptions, so pooling data is useful here because of the information and assumptions connecting the datasets.

For each set of conditions, the authors derive inverse probability weighted estimators for the identified parameters. These estimators use probability-based weights to account for missingness. Simulation studies and a data application evaluate the estimation strategies. The contribution links an identification argument to usable estimators, showing how an auxiliary source can resolve an ambiguity that persists within either dataset separately.
icml-2024-identification-and-estimation-.tldr: Under specified assumptions, combining two incomplete datasets can identify and estimate a parameter that neither dataset identifies alone.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing dataset, where actions outside the observed distribution can receive overly optimistic estimates. Restricting those actions can help, but rigid boundaries around the dataset's support may also hinder realistic estimates near the boundary. This paper seeks a more adaptive way to learn about nearby unseen data.

Adversarial data splitting, or ADS, creates distribution shifts within the available dataset. Its min-max procedure alternates between training a model on one subset to reduce loss on a validation subset and constructing a difficult split that maximizes the distribution shift and exposes generalization failures. The model is therefore trained against increasingly challenging differences between its training and validation data.

The authors derive a generalization error bound to help explain the framework and report extensive experiments supporting its effectiveness. The approach matters because it makes distribution shift part of the learning procedure itself. Rather than relying solely on a fixed distinction between observed and unobserved actions, ADS uses difficult internal splits to encourage generalization beyond the training subset.
icml-2024-improving-generalization-in-of.tldr: Adversarial data splitting improves offline reinforcement learning generalization by training against difficult distribution shifts constructed within the dataset.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a pretrained transformer use supplied examples to predict an answer for a new input. This paper investigates how that ability can extend across different kinds of mathematical functions. Its explanation connects transformers to neural networks that learn functions through approximate gradient descent.

The authors construct a family of transformers, using different activation functions, that implements approximate gradient updates on neural-network parameters. They also bound the required numbers of attention heads, hidden dimensions, and layers. Through neural-network approximations, they establish in-context learning constructions for linear functions, the function indicating membership in a unit ball, and smooth functions.

The analysis also considers a transformer pretrained on both linear regression and classification, proving that it can predict accurately on both tasks simultaneously. These are constructive capability results: they establish that suitable transformers can perform the described computations. Their significance is to extend the theoretical account of in-context learning beyond linear functions, with neural-network approximation providing the link to a broader range of function classes.
icml-2024-in-context-learning-on-functio.tldr: Constructive results show how transformers can learn several function classes in context by implementing approximate gradient descent on neural networks.

paragraphs: Complementary labels tell a learner which classes an example does not belong to. Existing statistically consistent methods have relied either on uniformly generated complementary labels or on ordinary labeled data to estimate how labels are produced. The paper addresses settings where those requirements may not hold.

Inspired by positive-unlabeled learning, the authors develop an unbiased risk estimator under a Selected-Completely-at-Random assumption. This offers a consistent approach without the two earlier requirements, while retaining its own assumption about label selection. A further risk-correction method addresses overfitting, connecting the statistical formulation to a practical training issue.

The paper also shows that a one-versus-rest formulation turns complementary-label learning into multiple negative-unlabeled binary classification problems. For each class, the available information identifies some examples as negatives while leaving others unlabeled. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets report improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution provides both an alternative statistical foundation and a useful connection to binary learning with incomplete labels.
icml-2024-learning-with-complementary-la.tldr: A complementary-label learning method achieves consistency under a Selected-Completely-at-Random assumption and adds risk correction to address overfitting.

paragraphs: A deployed language model typically remains fixed, which can make adding new knowledge difficult. MEMORYLLM explores a model design with a substantial portion of self-updatable parameters. The aim is to incorporate incoming text knowledge efficiently while retaining information supplied through earlier updates.

The architecture combines a transformer with a fixed-size memory pool inside its latent space. This makes updateable memory part of the model's internal representation. The central challenge is twofold: new information must become usable, and repeated updates must preserve the ability to use older information. The paper evaluates both aspects rather than treating successful knowledge insertion as the whole problem.

Model-editing benchmarks support the model's ability to incorporate new knowledge. Custom evaluations and long-context benchmarks also support long-term information retention. In addition, the authors report no observed performance degradation after nearly a million memory updates. That endurance result provides evidence that repeated updates can remain operationally stable in their evaluations, making the architecture relevant to language models whose knowledge needs to change after deployment.
icml-2024-memoryllm-towards-self-updatab.tldr: MEMORYLLM embeds an updateable memory pool in a transformer, showing knowledge integration and retention without observed degradation across nearly a million updates.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods can tackle continuous-control problems even when nonlinear dynamics create rough, nonsmooth optimization landscapes. This paper develops a mathematical explanation of how stochastic policies smooth those landscapes. The smoothing, called mollification, can make the objective easier to optimize and thereby help policy search.

The same mechanism has a cost: the stochastic objective moves further away from the original problem as smoothing increases. The authors establish an equivalence between policy gradient methods and solving backward heat equations. Because those equations are ill-posed in partial differential equation theory, the connection exposes a fundamental challenge for policy gradient methods operating under stochasticity.

The paper further relates this limitation to the uncertainty principle in harmonic analysis, using that connection to interpret exploration with stochastic policies. Experiments illustrate both the helpful and harmful effects of smoothing. The result is a framework for understanding a tradeoff within exploration: randomness can improve the optimization landscape while also changing the objective being optimized, so easier optimization does not by itself establish closer agreement with the original problem.
icml-2024-mollification-effects-of-polic.tldr: The paper explains how stochastic policy gradients smooth difficult objectives while introducing a fundamental tradeoff between optimization ease and fidelity to the original problem.

paragraphs: Federated reinforcement learning lets agents learn a shared policy without sharing their trajectory data. This paper considers agents whose environments may differ arbitrarily, extending beyond settings that require the environments to be identical or similar. The target is a common policy that performs well on average across the participating environments.

The authors introduce FedSVRPG-M and FedHAPG-M, two algorithms that use momentum. They prove that both can converge exactly to a stationary point of the average performance objective regardless of the magnitude of environment heterogeneity. A stationary point is the stated convergence target; the result does not establish that the algorithms always find a globally optimal policy.

By also using variance reduction or Hessian approximation, the algorithms achieve a reported sample complexity of O(ε^(-3/2)/N), where N is the number of agents. The inverse dependence on N gives a linear speedup with additional agents in the theoretical result. This demonstrates how collaboration can improve learning efficiency even when the agents contribute experience from substantially different environments.
icml-2024-momentum-for-the-win-collabora.tldr: Two momentum-based federated reinforcement learning algorithms converge to stationary points despite arbitrary environment heterogeneity and obtain linear speedups with more agents.

paragraphs: GANs can struggle with small training datasets because the discriminator overfits, degrading the learning signal supplied to the generator. This paper examines that signal directly. The authors observe that, with limited data, the gradient patterns received by the generator become increasingly aggregated as training proceeds.

They interpret the observation using renormalization group ideas from physics. The aggregated gradient pattern differs strongly from its coarse-grained versions, suggesting a sensitive, high-capacity system vulnerable to overfitting and collapse. Their proposed MS³D regularizer constrains the gradient field to maintain a consistent pattern across multiple scales. The intended effect is a more redundant and robust learning signal.

The authors report improved GAN performance and training stability in limited-data settings, including generation of high-quality images from very few examples. The contribution focuses attention on the structure of the discriminator's gradients across scales. It provides evidence that regularizing this structure can help the generator learn more effectively when the amount of training data leaves the discriminator especially prone to overfitting.
icml-2024-ms-3-d-a-rg-flow-based-regular.tldr: MS³D regularizes discriminator gradients for consistency across scales, improving GAN stability and image generation when training data is scarce.

paragraphs: Ad hoc teamwork requires an agent to cooperate with teammates without prior coordination or joint training. Open ad hoc teamwork adds another difficulty: the number of teammates can change. A learner must therefore handle variation in both who participates and how many agents are present.

Graph-based policy learning, or GPL, offers a practical approach because graph neural networks can accommodate varying numbers and types of agents. However, the paper identifies a gap in the explanation of GPL's joint Q-value representation over a coordination graph. This representation concerns the value of collective actions, making its justification central to understanding how the approach learns cooperation.

The authors develop a theory of that representation and its learning procedure using cooperative game theory. Building on this account, they introduce CIAO, an algorithm within the GPL framework that includes additional theoretically supported implementation techniques intended to facilitate learning. The contribution connects a practical architecture for changing teams to a clearer mathematical foundation and uses that foundation to motivate algorithmic changes.
icml-2024-open-ad-hoc-teamwork-with-coop.tldr: CIAO uses cooperative game theory to justify and improve graph-based policy learning for cooperation with unfamiliar, changing teams.

paragraphs: Score-based causal discovery compares candidate causal structures according to how well they fit observations. A generalized scoring approach uses a reproducing kernel Hilbert space to accommodate varied distributions and relationships. Its effectiveness depends on the kernel, but choosing kernel parameters manually can be tedious and may fail to find the best fit.

This paper makes kernel selection automatic within the causal graph search. At each search step, the authors model the generative process for the relevant variables as a mixture of independent noise variables. From this model, they derive a selection procedure that maximizes the variables' marginal likelihood. The chosen kernel is therefore tied to a data-fitting objective at that particular search step.

Experiments on synthetic data and real-world benchmarks show improvements over heuristic kernel selection. The approach matters because kernel choice directly affects how the score characterizes relationships, and consequently how candidate graph structures are assessed. Its optimality is expressed through the proposed likelihood criterion; the empirical results support its usefulness for the causal discovery comparisons performed.
icml-2024-optimal-kernel-choice-for-scor.tldr: An automatic marginal-likelihood procedure selects kernels during causal graph search and outperforms heuristic kernel choices in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Learning a new environment quickly while retaining old navigation skills combines two demands that machine learning systems often struggle to satisfy together. The authors introduce the sequential Morris Water Maze to study this combination. It extends an established psychology and neuroscience task so that success requires both rapid adaptation and continual learning.

Their model combines three biologically motivated ingredients. A content-addressable memory separates structural knowledge shared across environments, represented by grid cells, from environment-specific information represented by hippocampal cells. A spatially invariant convolutional architecture supports rapid adaptation. Remapping makes internal representations orthogonal, supporting continued learning without forgetting earlier environments.

On the proposed task, the model outperforms neural-network baselines drawn from continual learning and retains prior environment knowledge while learning to navigate new ones rapidly. The results connect the memory design to generalization, the convolutional architecture to adaptation, and remapping to retention. They support this particular combination of biological ideas as a promising route toward systems that transfer knowledge quickly while preserving earlier skills.
icml-2024-rapid-learning-without-catastr.tldr: A biologically inspired navigation model combines shared structure, environment-specific memory, and remapping to learn new mazes quickly while retaining old ones.

paragraphs: Scientific reasoning benchmarks often emphasize high-school material and elementary algebra. SciBench broadens the evaluation to college-level mathematics, chemistry, and physics. Its purpose is to examine the abilities needed for more complex scientific problem solving through a carefully curated collection of problems across these domains.

The authors evaluate representative open-source and proprietary language models with several prompting strategies. The best overall score in their study is 43.22%, indicating substantial difficulty for the evaluated models. A detailed user study also organizes the models' errors into ten problem-solving abilities, giving a more informative view of performance than an overall score alone.

The prompting comparison finds no strategy that significantly outperforms the others overall. Some strategies improve particular abilities while reducing performance on others. This means prompt changes can produce uneven gains across the skills involved in scientific reasoning. SciBench contributes both a harder evaluation setting and an analysis of where performance breaks down, providing a basis for studying improvements in scientific problem solving.
icml-2024-scibench-evaluating-college-le.tldr: SciBench tests college-level scientific reasoning, finding a best evaluated score of 43.22% and no prompting strategy with a significant overall advantage.

paragraphs: State-space models are used to learn relationships across sequences, but this paper shows that their long-term memory depends on how their parameters are represented. Without reparameterization, the authors prove that relationships these models can stably approximate must have memory that decays exponentially. This resembles a limitation of traditional recurrent neural networks.

The analysis traces this curse of memory to recurrent weights approaching a stability boundary. The authors introduce a class of reparameterizations that lifts the identified memory limitation. Changing the parameterization addresses how the model represents its recurrent dynamics, making it possible to improve the set of relationships it can stably approximate.

The paper also shows that a principled choice of reparameterization can improve optimization stability, so the benefit extends beyond representational capability. Experiments on synthetic datasets, language modeling, and image classification validate the findings. The main implication is that long-memory limitations are not solely a question of choosing a state-space architecture: parameterization itself can determine both stable approximation and the behavior of training.
icml-2024-stablessm-alleviating-the-curs.tldr: StableSSM uses reparameterization to lift a proven stable-memory limitation of state-space models and can also improve optimization stability.

paragraphs: Researchers often want to assess how much a feature matters for a classification outcome while accounting for other variables. This paper introduces expected total variation, or ETV, as a deterministic measure of that importance. The measure itself is defined without making assumptions about a predictive model.

The authors then develop Total Variation Floodgate algorithms for statistical inference about ETV under design-based or model-X assumptions. Those assumptions belong to the inference procedure, even though the underlying importance measure is model-free. The algorithms can use any regression function chosen by the user and produce asymptotic lower confidence bounds on the importance quantity.

A lower confidence bound provides a statistically qualified floor on importance, rather than only a point estimate. Its asymptotic nature means the stated confidence behavior concerns the large-sample setting. Simulations and a conjoint-analysis case study concerning a US general election demonstrate the algorithms' effectiveness. The work separates the definition of variable importance from the predictive tool used to help estimate it, while making uncertainty part of the reported conclusion.
icml-2024-total-variation-floodgate-for-.tldr: Total Variation Floodgate provides asymptotic lower confidence bounds for a model-free classification importance measure under design-based or model-X assumptions.

paragraphs: Heterophilous graphs connect nodes to dissimilar neighbors, but that description covers many different connection patterns. This paper develops a random graph model that accommodates those patterns and uses it to analyze graph convolution within fully connected networks. The central question is how the connections affect the ability to separate nodes.

The analysis identifies two factors governing separability gains: the Euclidean distance between neighborhood distributions and the square root of average node degree. It also shows that inconsistent neighborhoods reduce separability, with an effect comparable to lowering the effective average degree. Thus, the arrangement and consistency of neighbors matter alongside the number of connections.

For multiple layers, separability gains depend on normalized distances between neighborhood distributions propagated through the corresponding number of steps. This yields regimes where nodes remain separable even when oversmoothing occurs. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the theory. The findings give a more specific explanation of heterophily than treating all connections between dissimilar nodes as equally problematic for graph neural networks.
icml-2024-understanding-heterophily-for-.tldr: A theoretical model explains how neighborhood patterns, degree, inconsistency, and depth determine node separability in heterophilous graph neural networks.

paragraphs: Compact vision transformers still spend computation on the feature channels used by attention and feedforward components. This paper proposes DCS-Transformer, a block that learns differentiable channel selection. Selection operates in attention-weight computation and in the input and output features of the block's multilayer perceptron.

The design is motivated by the information bottleneck framework. The authors derive a variational upper bound for the information bottleneck loss that can be optimized with stochastic gradient descent, then add it to the network's training objective. This connects the learned channel selection to an explicit optimization criterion rather than treating compactness only as a fixed architecture choice.

In experiments, the authors replace all transformer blocks in MobileViT and EfficientViT with DCS-Transformer blocks. Results on image classification and object detection show reduced floating-point computation while maintaining or improving prediction accuracy, with some comparisons reporting much better accuracy. The contribution is a compatible replacement block that makes channel selection trainable and demonstrates favorable accuracy and computation tradeoffs across the evaluated visual architectures.
icml-2024-visual-transformer-with-differ.tldr: DCS-Transformer learns channel selection through an information-bottleneck-inspired objective, reducing visual transformer computation while maintaining or improving evaluated accuracy.
